## Should I use AI for this task?

Two questions decide how much to trust AI with a task:

1.  **Stakes** - how costly is it if the output is wrong and nobody notices?
2.  **Verifiability** - how quickly and reliably can *you* check the output?

## Stakes and verifiability

|  | **Easy to verify** | **Hard to verify** |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **Low stakes** | **Just use it.** Reformat a sample sheet, draft a figure legend, explain an error message. | **Use it loosely.** Brainstorming or drafting a document. Treat it as a starting point only. |
| **High stakes** | **Use it, then check it.** Have it write code to count rows, then compare with a spreadsheet filter. Check gene IDs against Ensembl. | **Don't rely on it alone.** Choosing the statistical test, deciding which samples to exclude, interpreting the biology. Read up or talk to a bioinformatician. |

# Good workflows {background-color="#23373B" .center .middle}

## What is a good AI workflow

A good AI workflow for bioinformatics largely replicates a good bioinformatics workflow without AI. As with how we code more traditionally, taking short-cuts comes back to haunt us later. Very little of Bioinformatics is just 'plug and play'.

Key cornerstones:

- Planning
- Reproducibility
- Checkpoints and Review

## What is a good AI workflow

A core principle of working with the LLM is being the driver. It is easy to be a passenger. The more you yield decision-making and executive control to these tools, the more chance that mistakes happen. 

If at any point you feel out of your depth or if the analysis starts to feel like a black box, that is when you need to reach out for support from your friendly neighborhood bioinformatician. 

## Getting Started

Open up Claude Code or OpenAI Codex and start a new project. 

The folder you provide will define the scope. This means where on your computer it will have access to. You will also want to add any files there you want it to be able to read. 

# Planning {background-color="#23373B" .center .middle}

## Planning

To start with we need to make decisions about how we will address our problem.

**For example:**

*"I have some scRNAseq data from mouse fat cells. I want to generate clusters of fat cell sub types"*

At this point you can decide what software to use (Seurat/Scanpy) and what reference to use (mm10/mm39). 

Having a plan is important from the outset. If you are unfamiliar with the analysis the broad-stroked planning is the opportunity to start understanding what are the conceptual steps in the analysis. That way you can keep your hands on the wheel.

## Planning

Working collaboratively with the LLMs to make an analysis plan document is a good place to start. This will help break down your broad objectives into smaller tasks.

**For example:**

*"I have some scRNAseq data from mouse fat cells. I want to do some generate clusters of fat cell sub types. I want help building an analysis workflow. First though we will work together to make key decisions like software and which analysis steps are required. In the process I want to make an analysis plan document broken down into the key steps for the workflow"*

There are several skills which can also help with this process like /grill and /plan. 

## Planning

You can use LLMs to help with planning, but as always, do not take it purely at face value. Validate with trusted sources. Remember the context of your experiment is everything and tools can be fickle. 

It is ultimately up to you to decide what is the best approach.

i.e. scRNAseq has a pretty standard QC workflow, but there are many edge cases:

- Cell cycle regression can remove real signal in post-mitotic Neurons
- Standard filters will vary between snRNA and scRNAseq
- Relaxed filtering may be necessary to detect rare cell types

# Reproducibility {background-color="#23373B" .center .middle}

## Reproducibility

LLMs in general are not reproducible. If I ask the same prompt multiple times I will get different responses. 

Say I had perfectly copied my context so that someone could replicate my work they may struggle to use the identical model. Frontier models like those from Claude and ChatGPT, do update and are then retired with limited to access them. 

**If this is the state of play how do you stay reproducible?**

## Reproducibility

There are two aspects that are most important to ensure that you stay reproducible.

* Manage and save your software versions
* Always make code

The LLMs should not be covertly running code and making plots without it also saving that code and saving how or where this was ran. This is the most important step that we see skipped by people doing their own LLM-supported analysis.

## Managing software

It doesn't matter if you are running code in R, python, shell scripts etc. What matters is that you have static versions of these software and the packages they use across your analysis. This means once you start on a project you **do not** update the software. 

You can use package managers like Conda/Mamba or create containers like Dockers to help manage your software and also enable you to share these with other people or other systems i.e. HPC. We have a whole course on reproducibility including software management [here](https://rockefelleruniversity.github.io/RU_reproducibleR/)

You do not need to do this alone though. Setting up these software environments is something that Claude and ChatGPT are pretty good at. Once you are set up you can ensure it takes an appropriate snapshot, then you are good to go. 

## Always make code

Once you have your software the next step is code. You can easily prompt code generation by simply asking for it.

Especially when working on my laptop I will have a folder in which I will have data, results and the code which links the two. 

If we are using Claude Code or Codex, these files will be generated in your project. 

Ideally you would be using Git and Github as you go to manage version control. Again Claude can help with this. 

# Checkpoints and Review {background-color="#23373B" .center .middle}

## Checkpoints

As we mentioned with strengths and limitation we don't necessarily want to do everything at once for two main reasons:

  * It's easier for the LLMs to get overwhelmed by the scale of the task.
  * It's easier for the user to skip essential checkpoints and tests. 

## Checkpoints

If you are trying something for the first time or working on something exploratory this is checkpoints are even more important. The key part is to evaluate code line-by-line and review the outcomes. You should hopefully have technical and biological expectations about the data as it is processed.

For example:

  * How many rows should the matrix have?
  * Should it be logged?
  * What distribution should the data have?
  * Should a marker gene be expressed in one sample and not the other?

## What should I do if I can't read the code

If you do not understand the code that you are generating take some extra time and break it down. Just because it runs, does not mean it is doing what you want it to do. 

Here are some suggested steps are based on key principles in coding and Bioinformatics that we use when we run new tools or languages we are unfamiliar with. 

* **Ask for annotation of the code** - Once annotated read the overviews and ask questions (not just to the LLMs). Add your own additional annotations to help fill in the gaps or correct mistakes.

* **Run it** - If code is wrong, it often errors or gives warnings. If it runs, check the output is right. If you don't know what right looks like then you need some positive controls and trial datasets. If it gives warnings, double-check why. 

* **Look it up** - Check arguments against the package help and vignettes. Check anytime it points you to a paper. Review the core principles of your analysis

## What should I do if I can't read the code 

* **Start small** - Only use a small amount of the data. You do not need to run all the data at once. Make sure you understand it first so you know it is doing what is is supposed to be doing. 

* **Double-check what it is actually doing** - As you work through chunks of code, check the saved variables. Do they look as expected? If not, why?

* **Verify the numbers** - Does it make sense? Export results to spreadsheets so you can manually review. Do directions of changes make sense? Does the normalization make sense? Compare to plots and visualizations.

- **Cross-check** - Ask in a fresh session, or a different model, and compare. Disagreement means look carefully.

You remain responsible for everything the LLMs produce.

# Other things to consider {background-color="#23373B" .center .middle}

## Managing resources

When you are building scripts and planning something that is a little more computationally intensive you should also consider the resources you have available to you. Either on your laptop or on remote servers i.e. HPC systems. 

Already we suggest running your analysis on a subset to start, so you can make sure the code itself runs ok.

Once you have functioning code and are ready to run everything, then you should provide information about your computational setup so LLMs can adapt the code to your limits. 

## Building Reports

We work with reports as the hub for our deliverable analysis. Reports enable us to tie code directly to our output figures in fixed documents. This means no orphan plots where we're not sure exactly how they were generated. 

Popular examples include Quarto, Rmarkdown and Jupyter.

## The analysis loop: one step at a time

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  P["1 Plan<br/>plan.md"] --> E["2 Pin environment<br/>environment.yml / renv.lock"]
  E --> M

  subgraph LOOP ["Repeat for every step (e.g. QC, filtering, normalization, clustering, DE)"]
    direction LR
    M["3 Pick the next step<br/>write what you expect to see"] --> C["4 Generate code<br/>scripts/"]
    C --> S["5 Run on a subset<br/>logs/"]
    S --> U["6 Understand the code<br/>and check the output"]
    U --> D{"Does it make sense<br/>and do you understand it?"}
    D -- "no: fix or ask" --> C
    D -- "yes" --> UP["7 Update the plan<br/>record what you learned<br/>and re-decide the next step"]
    UP -. "back to the plan" .-> M
  end

  UP -- "all modules done" --> F["8 Scale up<br/>full data"]
  F --> R["9 Report<br/>report.qmd + model ID"]

  classDef step fill:#ffffff,stroke:#EB811B,stroke-width:2px,color:#000000
  classDef setup fill:#23373B,stroke:#23373B,color:#ffffff
  classDef check fill:#EB811B,stroke:#EB811B,color:#000000
  classDef done fill:#2E8B57,stroke:#2E8B57,color:#ffffff
  class P,E setup
  class M,C,S,U,UP step
  class D check
  class F,R done
  style LOOP fill:#f4f4f4,stroke:#23373B,stroke-width:2px
```

## Good practice still applies

To summarize, even when we have LLM-assisted coding, good coding practice is still essential. If you lean on vibe-coding an analysis it opens the door to mistakes. 

- Planning
- Reproducibility
- Checkpoints and Review

Ultimately you still need to understand what the analysis is doing, how it is doing it, and why it is doing that. Through this you keep your hands on the wheel. If this is too much reach out to your friendly neighborhood bioinformatician for help. 

# Bad Practice {background-color="#23373B" .center .middle}

## Who is driving?

A repeated analogy we have used is "who is driving?". It is very easy to give away our control.

Claude code generally tries to make this danger clear i.e. the full permissions CLI mode is called "--dangerously-skip-permissions".

That said we can achieve something similar with a much less scary prompt:

*Complete a scRNAseq analysis on this mouse PBMC dataset. If there are errors fix them. Keep going until you finish.*

## Controlling what is allowed

As we give more capabilities and autonomy to the LLMs we will also need clearly defined limits.  

Many of us may have data that we do not want shared with LLMs and/or files that we want to protect from Agents i.e. personal data, raw files, logins etc.

When we start a project in Claude Code or Codex this sets the scope of the project. In theory this should prevent it interacting outside of this. 

## Controlling what is allowed

In the context section we saw that CLAUDE.md/Agents.md can only *ask* the agent to stay away from specific directories, functions or methods: they are guides.

To outright ban them, use [settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#permissions) permissions or hooks, which the harness enforces.

Examples: [project settings.json](https://github.com/RockefellerUniversity/responsible_use_of_AI_for_noncoders/blob/master/docs/data/claude_examples/project/.claude/settings.json){target="_blank"} · [a hook that protects raw data](https://github.com/RockefellerUniversity/responsible_use_of_AI_for_noncoders/blob/master/docs/data/claude_examples/project/.claude/hooks/protect-raw.sh){target="_blank"}

## Hard lines

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  subgraph ROW [" "]
    direction LR
    AI["AI proposes an action<br/>e.g. delete files, install packages"]
    L1["Layer 1<br/>CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md<br/><i>advisory: can be ignored or lost in a long session</i>"]
    L2["Layer 2<br/>Permission settings and deny rules<br/><i>enforced by the app</i>"]
    L3["Layer 3<br/>Human review<br/>"]
    OK(["Safe outcome"])
    AI --> L1 --> L2 --> L3 --> OK
  end

  subgraph BASE [" "]
    NET["<div style='width:640px'>SAFETY NET: backups · git history · read-only raw data<br/><i>if every layer above fails, you can undo it</i></div>"]
  end

  ROW ~~~ BASE

  classDef ai fill:#EB811B,stroke:#EB811B,color:#000000
  classDef layer fill:#ffffff,stroke:#EB811B,stroke-width:2px,color:#000000
  classDef human fill:#23373B,stroke:#23373B,color:#ffffff
  classDef net fill:#2F6FA8,stroke:#2F6FA8,color:#ffffff
  classDef ok fill:#2E8B57,stroke:#2E8B57,color:#ffffff
  class AI ai
  class L1,L2 layer
  class L3 human
  class NET net
  class OK ok
  style ROW fill:none,stroke:none
  style BASE fill:none,stroke:none
```

## LLMs find a way

The way we instruct these tools can accidentally give them freedom beyond what we allow. It doesn't have to be as expliocit as prior examples. 

For example:

"Lets do the *next step in the analysis*"
"Give me the code for *this figure*" 

In both these cases I though I was being explicit and we had a pattern of step-wise interrogation, action and review. Instead it took this as permissive instructions for it to conduct an entire analysis, or to add the code for a given figure directly into my analysis report.

## Hard lines can be softer than you think

Similarly we have seen hard lines which have been set flouted for similar semantic reasons i.e. do not interact with the HPC or do not commit anything without my review.

This happens despite these limits being saved in CLAUDE.md files.
